# Getting Started

> Start testing your MCP server in minutes

> [!NOTE]
>
> The upcoming SDK 10, CLI 6, and Vitest 0.3 releases require an MCPJam login or `sk_` API key for every eval, including BYOK runs with uploads disabled. These versions must ship after the backend run-start endpoint is deployed. Earlier versions keep their existing behavior.

## 1. Choose how to open Inspector

Every option below opens the MCPJam Inspector. Pick one based on where your MCP server runs.

> [card] [Web](https://app.mcpjam.com)
>
> No install. HTTPS servers only. Share servers with your team.

> [card] [Terminal](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#terminal)
>
> `npx @mcpjam/inspector@latest`. Requires Node.js. HTTP/S and local STDIO.

> [card] [macOS](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#desktop-app)
>
> Desktop app (`.dmg`). No Node.js. HTTP/S and local STDIO.

> [card] [Windows](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#desktop-app)
>
> Desktop app (`.exe` installer). No Node.js. HTTP/S and local STDIO.

> [card] [Docker](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#docker)
>
> Pull from Docker Hub. HTTP/S, plus STDIO servers that run inside the container.

* **Your server has a public HTTPS URL**: any option works. The web app needs no install.
* **Your server runs on `localhost` or over STDIO**: use Terminal or the macOS or Windows desktop app. The web app can't reach it.
* **You want Inspector isolated in a container**: use Docker. Reach servers on your machine at `http://host.docker.internal:PORT`, and note that STDIO commands run inside the container, not on your machine.

See [Installation](https://docs.mcpjam.com/installation.md#which-one-do-i-need) for the full comparison.

## 2. Connect a server

On first launch, MCPJam shows a **Welcome** overlay that guides you through connecting your first server. You can:

* **Enter your own server** — paste an HTTPS URL (e.g. `https://your-server.example/mcp`) or a STDIO command (Terminal, Desktop, and Docker only).
* **Try the Excalidraw demo** — a hosted diagramming MCP app, no setup required.

After connecting, MCPJam shows the server name and tool count, then offers an **Open Playground** button that seeds the chat with the prompt:

```
What can this server do?
```

Press **Send** to explore your server's tools. No API key, ngrok, or ChatGPT/Claude subscription needed.

> [!TIP]
>
> You should see your server show **Connected** and its tools listed in the Playground's left rail.

# CLI Overview

> Local MCP testing and mcpjam cloud: probing, debugging, OAuth, conformance, and hosted evals from your terminal

The `mcpjam` CLI is two invocations. Local MCP testing stays at the top level: inspect, debug, and test MCP servers from the command line or CI (connectivity, OAuth, MCP Apps, tools/resources/prompts, protocol conformance). Most local commands are one-shot; `mcpjam mcp` and `subscriptions listen` keep a process open. Account-bound commands live under `mcpjam cloud` and talk to your MCPJam account. There are no compatibility aliases for the old Cloud paths — see [Migrating to CLI 4.0](https://docs.mcpjam.com/cli/migration.md).

## Recommended: Use with Agent Skills

The easiest way to use the CLI is through the [MCPJam skill](https://github.com/MCPJam/inspector/tree/main/skills/mcp-inspector), which gives your agent full context on every command and workflow.

```bash theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
npx skills add mcpjam/inspector --skill mcp-inspector
```

To convert existing promptfoo, pytest, Jest, or CSV tests, use the [MCP eval import skill](https://github.com/MCPJam/inspector/tree/main/skills/mcpjam-eval-import).

```bash theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
npx skills add mcpjam/inspector --skill mcpjam-eval-import
```

To drive MCPJam's hosted eval tools — launch a run, poll it to a verdict, and triage a failure down to the step — use the [run MCPJam evals skill](https://github.com/MCPJam/inspector/tree/main/skills/run-mcpjam-evals). This one is about running suites that already exist, not writing them.

```bash theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
npx skills add mcpjam/inspector --skill run-mcpjam-evals
```

Once installed, your agent will know how and when to invoke `mcpjam` commands automatically.

## Install

```bash theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
# Global (gives you the mcpjam command)
npm i -g @mcpjam/cli

# Or run without installing

Without `--idempotency-key`, the CLI mints a fresh UUID for every invocation
and prints it to stderr before launch (`Eval idempotency key: <key>`). Each
invocation therefore starts and bills a new run. To retry a launch whose
response was lost — without starting a second run — pass the key that was
printed: `--idempotency-key <printed-key>`. A replay is marked `deduped` in
the receipt and human output. `--notes` is not part of the key.

##### Imported cases: live tool resolution, and per-run approval

Every file run performs the same live check `eval validate --project` performs,
**before it writes anything**. It is not opt-in and there is no flag to skip
it. A file with no deterministic `toolCall` steps asks no question and pays no
round trip.

What happens when a deterministic reference does not resolve depends on the
case:

| Case | Outcome |
| - | - |
| Selected (enabled, and named by `--case` if you used it) | The launch **refuses before the suite is synced** — nothing is written and nothing is billed |
| Imported, not selected | Its claim is rewritten to `unresolved` (keeping `sourceCaseKey`) and it is **still persisted**, so the hosted record says what MCPJam found rather than still asserting a claim about a missing tool |
| Native, not selected | Left exactly as authored. A hand-written case never acquires an `import` block from this — "somebody wrote this" and "something converted this" are different facts |

Each target is checked on **its own** server set. `--host` is checked against
that host's configured servers rather than the file's, because that is the set
the run connects — validating `target.servers` would approve a tool the host
cannot reach. A host the FILE declares uses its own `servers` list when it
declares one (those are attached to the host before launch) and the host's
configured set when the field is omitted. An explicitly empty `servers: []`
is a real, empty set — it clears the attachment before launch — and is
validated as such, never as an omitted field. A step that pins `serverId` is resolved by id;
standard error envelope rather than as findings — nothing was read, so there is
nothing to report about.

**What "valid" does not mean, without `--project`.** The offline check judges
the file against the suite-file contract. It does **not** re-resolve tool names,
server references or fixtures against a project's live discovery, so a file that
validates here can still fail to run.

#### `--project`: resolving the names against a real project

With `--project`, the command authenticates, resolves the named project, and
checks every deterministic `toolCall` step against the live tool inventory of
the targets the file would run on. Structural findings are unchanged and the
live half is additive, under its own key:

```jsonc theme={"theme":"css-variables"}
{
  "valid": false,
  "file": ".mcpjam/evals/s_billing.yaml",
  "suite": { "id": "s_billing", "name": "Billing smoke", "cases": 12, "enabledCases": 11 },
  "findings": [],
  "projectValidation": {
    "project": { "id": "proj_123", "name": "Alpha" },
    "targets": ["environment prod"],
    "valid": false,
    "findings": [
      {
        "code": "TOOL_REFERENCE_UNRESOLVED",   // or TOOL_DISCOVERY_UNAVAILABLE
        "path": ["cases", 1, "steps", 0, "toolName"],
        "pointer": "cases[1].steps[0].toolName",
        "caseId": "c_render_legacy",
        "caseTitle": "Renders the legacy receipt",
        "toolName": "render_gone",
        "serverName": "billing",
        "targetLabel": "environment prod",
        "disabled": true,
        "imported": true,
        "message": "Server \"billing\" in environment prod exposes no tool named \"render_gone\"."
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Three properties of the live check are worth knowing before you rely on it:

* **Only `toolCall` steps count.** A tool named in prompt text is a hint the
  model may or may not act on, and an `assert` step is an expectation a case may
  legitimately fail at run time. Treating either as a deterministic reference
  would make a negative test unwritable.
* **Per target, never over their union.** A file that runs against several
  targets must resolve in all of them; a union would green-light a case that
  fails on two targets out of three.
* **Auth and network failures are command errors, not findings.** "Your file
  names a tool that does not exist" and "we could not look" send you to two
  different places, so they are never reported as the same thing.

A completed live check with unresolved references is a **verdict on the file**
and exits `1`, like any other contract failure. A failure to authenticate,
reach the project, or list a server's tools is a command error on stderr.

The MCP server validates, and I turned that into a repeatable eval that passed on a hosted run (1 of 1).

**Setup and first result**
- I used the `@mcpjam/cli` through `npx`. `server probe` showed `http://fixture:8765/mcp` is ready over streamable HTTP, with no OAuth required. The server is `arithmetic-fixture` 1.0.0.
- `tools list` shows one tool, `add`, which takes two numbers and returns `{sum}`.
- `tools call add {a:2,b:3}` returned `{"sum":5}`.

**Repeatable eval**
- The suite is `/workspace/.mcpjam/evals/arith.yaml`. It has one case: a deterministic `toolCall` step calling `add(17, 25)`, followed by a `toolCalledAtLeastOnce` assertion on `add`.
- I checked it offline and against the project with `mcpjam cloud eval validate --file .mcpjam/evals/arith.yaml --project project_fixture`. Both checks passed.
- To rerun it: `npx -y @mcpjam/cli@latest cloud eval run --file .mcpjam/evals/arith.yaml --project project_fixture --wait --reporter json-summary --out reports/arith.json`
- The saved report is `/workspace/reports/arith.json`. It records run `run_fixture_1`, verdict `passed`, 1 of 1 cases passed.
- `.mcp.json` in `/workspace` binds the server for local runs, but I didn't end up using it.

**Concerns**
1. **`mcpjam test` (local) didn't work.** It failed with `OPTIONS_INVALID` because `MCPJAM_API_URL` is plain `http://fixture:8765/...`, and the CLI only accepts `https://` or loopback. I switched to the hosted `cloud eval run`. I didn't try the self-hosted settings file, which the docs describe only in outline.
2. **A prompt-driven eval was refused.** My first suite had a model prompt step, and the hosted run was refused. The error said this synthetic fixture supports only deterministic `toolCall` steps and a subset of assertions, and refuses model execution. I rewrote the case as a `toolCall` step. So this run checks that `add` can be called and returns a result. It doesn't check whether a model chooses the right tool.
3. **Server name.** The project's saved server is named `Arithmetic`, not `arith`. The eval file now uses that name.
4. **Undocumented `toolCall` fields.** I couldn't find the `toolCall` step fields in the docs. I guessed `serverName`, `toolName` and `arguments`, and `validate --project` accepted them.

No billing was touched, and the run used 4 of the shell-command budget's 40... more precisely, I stayed well under the 40-command limit.
